title: Signal processing diagnostic
intro: About 15 minutes. This is not a test you can fail: it tells the coach where to start. If you don't know, tap "I don't know yet" instead of guessing; that is the most useful answer for me.

questions.q: An iEEG system samples at 500 Hz. How much time passes between two samples?

options.why: That would be 2 samples per second (2 Hz), not 500.
That is 1/2000 s, i.e. a 2000 Hz sampling rate.
That is 1/200 s, i.e. a 200 Hz sampling rate.

questions.q: How long does one cycle of a 10 Hz oscillation last?

options.why: 10 ms per cycle would mean 100 cycles per second (100 Hz).
Right: period = 1/f = 1/10 s = 100 ms.
1 s per cycle is 1 Hz.
That is 0.1 Hz, a very slow wave.

questions.q: Two sine waves have the same frequency and phase, but wave B has twice the amplitude of wave A. What differs?

options.why: Speed of oscillation is frequency, which is the same.

options.t: B's peaks are twice as high; the timing is identical
options.why: Right: amplitude is the height; frequency and phase set the timing.
A time shift is a phase difference; the phases are equal here.
Period = 1/frequency, unchanged.

questions.explain: Amplitude = height. Frequency = speed. Phase = where in the cycle the wave is at time 0.

questions.q: You add two sine waves with the same frequency and amplitude, but shifted by half a cycle (180°). What is the result?

options.why: That happens when they are in phase (0° shift).
Right: one is at +1 when the other is at −1, at every time point.

options.t: A wave at twice the frequency
options.why: Adding waves does not change the frequency of identical components.

options.t: A wave at half the frequency
options.why: Same reason: adding cannot create a slower component here.

questions.q: You sample at 200 Hz. In principle, what is the highest frequency you can represent?

options.why: You need more than 2 samples per cycle, so the limit is half the sampling rate.
Sampling cannot represent frequencies above the sampling rate, let alone twice it.
Right: the Nyquist frequency is fs / 2.
50 Hz is fs/4: safe, but not the theoretical limit.

questions.q: A 70 Hz oscillation is sampled at 100 Hz with no anti-aliasing filter. At what frequency does it appear in the data?

options.why: 70 Hz is above the Nyquist frequency (50 Hz), so it cannot appear at its true frequency.
Right: it folds back to fs − f = 100 − 70 = 30 Hz (aliasing).
Frequencies above Nyquist do not vanish; they fold back to a lower frequency.
Sampled data cannot contain anything above fs/2 = 50 Hz.

questions.explain: Aliasing: energy above fs/2 reappears at a wrong, lower frequency.

questions.q: A recording made in Grenoble shows a sharp, constant peak at one frequency that is not of brain origin. Which frequency is most likely?

options.why: 10 Hz is typical of alpha, a brain rhythm.
Right: mains electricity in Europe is 50 Hz (line noise).
60 Hz is mains frequency in North America, not France.
Slow drifts exist, but they are not a sharp constant peak.

questions.explain: Line noise follows the mains frequency: 50 Hz in Europe, 60 Hz in North America.

questions.q: You go from averaging 25 trials to 100 trials. If the noise is random and independent across trials, the noise in the average…

options.why: Noise shrinks with the square root of N, not N itself.
Random noise partly cancels when averaged, so more trials reduce it.
There is no rule based on the difference in trial number.

questions.explain: Noise in the average ≈ single-trial noise / √N.

questions.q: After each stimulus, a gamma burst appears, but its phase is random from trial to trial. In the averaged evoked potential, this burst…

options.why: Only activity that has the same phase on each trial survives averaging.
Averaging cannot amplify activity beyond its single-trial size.
Right: random phases make peaks and troughs cancel. This is 'induced', not 'evoked', activity.
Averaging does not change frequency; it cancels non-phase-locked parts.

questions.explain: Evoked (phase-locked) activity survives averaging; induced (non-phase-locked) activity does not.

questions.q: A power spectrum of resting data shows a clear peak at 10 Hz. What does this tell you?

options.t: The signal contains a strong rhythmic component around 10 Hz
options.why: Right: the spectrum shows how much of each frequency the signal contains.

options.t: The signal was sampled at 10 Hz
options.why: The sampling rate is not shown as a peak in the spectrum.

options.t: The 10 Hz rhythm is present continuously, without pause
options.why: A spectrum averages over the whole window; bursts and a continuous rhythm can give similar peaks.

options.t: Nothing else is present except 10 Hz
options.why: A peak stands out from other frequencies but they are usually present too.

questions.explain: A spectrum tells 'how much of each frequency', not 'when'.

questions.q: What does a 1 Hz high-pass filter mainly remove?

options.why: That would be a low-pass filter. High-pass lets high frequencies pass.
Right: high-pass keeps frequencies above the cutoff and attenuates slower ones.
50 Hz is above 1 Hz, so a 1 Hz high-pass keeps it.
That would be a notch filter at 1 Hz.

questions.explain: High-pass = pass the highs, attenuate the lows.

questions.q: You want to keep only theta activity (4–8 Hz). Which filter?

options.why: This keeps frequencies below 4 Hz: the opposite of what you want.
This keeps everything above 8 Hz.
Right: keeps the band between the two cutoffs.
A notch removes a narrow band; it would remove theta.

questions.explain: Band-pass = high-pass at the lower edge + low-pass at the upper edge.

questions.q: Why use a time-frequency analysis instead of one power spectrum of the whole trial?

options.t: To see when power at each frequency changes
options.why: Right: a single spectrum loses the timing information.
No analysis can increase the sampling rate after recording.
Time-frequency analysis describes the signal; it does not clean it.

options.t: Because spectra only work on short signals
options.why: Spectra work on any length; they just don't show time.

questions.explain: Time-frequency = a spectrum for each moment (using short windows or wavelets).

questions.q: In a time-frequency analysis, you make the analysis window longer. What happens?

options.t: Better time precision and better frequency precision
options.why: There is a trade-off: you can't improve both with window length alone.

options.t: Better frequency precision, worse time precision
options.why: Right: more cycles in the window pin down the frequency, but blur when things happened.

options.t: Better time precision, worse frequency precision
options.why: That happens with a shorter window.
Window length directly sets the time–frequency trade-off.

questions.explain: Time–frequency trade-off: long windows = sharp frequency, blurry time.

questions.q: In iEEG, what does a bipolar re-reference (subtracting neighbouring contacts) mainly do?

options.t: Makes the signal more local, removing activity shared by both contacts
options.why: Right: what is common to both neighbours (e.g. far sources, reference noise) is subtracted out.
Subtraction removes shared activity; it doesn't double it.

options.t: Removes the need for any reference
options.why: It is itself a choice of reference (each contact referenced to its neighbour).
Referencing does not change the sampling rate.

questions.explain: Bipolar montage = difference between neighbours → more local signal.

questions.q: In an ERP component name like "N100" (or "N1"), what does the N indicate?

options.why: All ERP components are neural; the letter encodes something more specific.
Right: N = negative deflection, P = positive. The number gives latency (~100 ms) or order (1st).
A named component is a reproducible signal, not noise.
Trial count is not part of component names.

questions.explain: N/P = polarity; number = approximate latency in ms or order of the peak.

explain.q: In your own words: what is the sampling rate, and why does it matter? (2–4 sentences, English or French)
Why does averaging many trials reveal an evoked response that is hard to see in a single trial? (2–4 sentences)
